In reality, Theranos hid malfunctioning tech, forged quality reports, and deceived patients and investors while silencing whistleblowers. The PR image was a calculated shield covering systemic corporate fraud and medical risk.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.05, -0.11) — Greater Evil

Documentaries like 'The Inventor' and 'You Can See Everything' contrast Holmes' cultivated public persona—curated voice, Steve Jobs attire, elite board backing—against the empirical reality of fake lab results and aggressive legal intimidation.

The fallout from Theranos exposed the dangers of Silicon Valley 'fake it till you make it' culture in medicine, forcing stronger regulatory oversight and investigative scrutiny over hype-driven biotech startups.

Holmes committed a Q1 Metaphysical and Q5 Logical Error. She swapped actual technical capability (WHAT) with curated messianic charisma (WHO), using elite political endorsements to substitute for falsifiable lab evidence.

Social Physics Analysis:
Holmes executed a classic Smart Selfish Loop. She manufactured a noble pretext (democratizing diagnostics) to extract capital and prestige, projecting fraud onto critics and using non-disclosure threats to enforce compliance.

By projecting a transformative future (+2,+2) to mask actual technical non-existence (-2,+2), the venture collapsed into systemic fraud.

The Unavoidable Truth: Charisma and powerful board members cannot alter the laws of chemistry or validate non-functioning medical hardware.

The Unavoidable Lie: Pretextual idealism excuses deceiving patients and concealing dangerous technological failures.

When narrative branding replaces empirical verification, institutional oversight decays into sycophancy. True innovation requires rigorous open auditing, not performative devotion.

Awwthekanon:
Real healthcare isn't born from vanity or corporate theater, but from honest care for human life. True healing comes when we value actual patient safety over personal ambitions and performative success.

Brothekanon:
Bro, fake turtlenecks and a deep voice don't make a blood scanner work. You can't fake it till you make it when real people's health is on the line. Accountability always comes due.

"For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, nor anything concealed that will not be known or brought out into the open." Luke 8:17 — FAIL
Deceit built on illusion inevitably crumbles when confronted by unyielding truth.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
What the other Elizabeth Holmes doc shows that ‘You Can See Everything’ doesn’t

Alex Gibney's 2019 documentary about the rise and fall of Holmes' tech startup Theranos serves as an insightful companion piece to Nathan Fielder's 'You Can See Everything.'

Actual Article Body:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.   Set us as preferred

Before “You Can See Everything” and before “The Dropout,” there was “The Inventor.”

Subtitled “Out for Blood in Silicon Valley,” Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and the rise and fall of her biotech company Theranos, which she vowed would revolutionize the blood-testing industry, is attracting renewed attention in the wake of the explosive response to “You Can See Everything.”

The new documentary, which captures the former CEO’s final days of freedom before beginning an 11-year prison sentence, presents Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in twisty, often uncomfortable interactions with comedian and co-director Nathan Fielder as he presses them about their relationship and her past with Theranos. Since its premiere last week and subsequent successful box office, awards season buzz has been escalating around the film, Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim.

While “You Can See Everything” is primarily an intimate portrait of an emotional Holmes at home with Evans and their two young children, “The Inventor,” which premiered on HBO in 2019, provides a different landscape, showing a laser-focused Holmes carrying out her singular directive to make Theranos a dominant force in preventive medicine.

Movies

The year’s most discussable film is finally in theaters and its many bizarre surprises don’t disappoint. Hold off on reading this until after you see it.

Gibney shows the photogenic Stanford dropout’s evolution into a major celebrity and tech power broker, rubbing shoulders with world leaders. Her quirks of wearing only black turtlenecks and her apparent disinterest in anything not related to her medical quest (“I don’t have any secrets,” she says early in the film) are also on full display.

The attention surrounding Holmes also sparked the release of the bestselling book “Bad Blood” by Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyrou, and “The Dropout,” a Hulu miniseries starring Amanda Seyfried. The actor, who won an Emmy for her portrayal of Holmes, is a significant presence in “You Can See Everything.”

“The Inventor” and “You Can See Everything” can now be positioned as cinematic bookends to the Holmes phenomenon. Here are major takeaways from the Gibney documentary, which provides additional insight into Holmes.

When Holmes first speaks, her bold voice is markedly different from the more casual tone in “You Can See Everything.” Insiders at Theranos spoke about how Holmes intentionally lowered her voice to sound less feminine in the male-dominated tech world.

Her intensely blue eyes are showcased at the pull-focus feature of her face. Staffers interviewed in the film say  they noticed that Holmes never blinked, which they found unusual and somewhat intimidating.

Holmes frequently related how she grew up spending summers and holidays with her uncle, who she adored. She recalled how much he loved the beach, and was devastated when he was diagnosed with skin cancer, which transitioned into brain cancer. “I never got to say goodbye.”

Her grief ignited her desire to want to change the world so that  everyone would have access to their personal health information, “a world in which no one has to say, ‘If only I had known sooner.’”

She developed an interest for creating things at a young age, including plans for building a time machine when she was 7, she told New Yorker writer Ken Auletta. Through her early school and high school years, “I never really watched TV. My best friends were books,” singling out  “The Iliad” and “Moby-Dick.”

She also spoke of her long-standing terror of needles, calling it “torture” when she had to give blood.

“When she was talking about some subject other than diagnostic testing, she was very unprepossessing, very disingenuous,” said Fortune magazine reporter Roger Parloff. “When she began to talk about the mission, or you know, her business, then there was a shift. She became very focused, very intense, firm, in control of all of the facts. No question surprised her, very impressive and idealistic.”

This mesmerizing showdown is the King Kong vs. Godzilla of con artists as ‘The Rehearsal’s’ Nathan Fielder tries to wrestle the truth out of Theranos’ Elizabeth Holmes.

Holmes reveals the reasons behind her wardrobe, which is exclusively black. Saying she wants to give “every bit of energy I have” to Theranos, Holmes shows off her closet, which contains black jackets and turtlenecks.

“I have these exact set of clothes so I don’t have to think about it,” she said. Part of her reasoning is due to her hero, former Apple CEO Steve Jobs, although she points out that Jobs wore blue jeans.

She adds that she had been wearing black turtlenecks since she was 7.

Auletta details how Holmes’ apartment was basically just a mattress. “The only thing in her refrigerator was bottled water. She ate all her meals at the office. She slept four hours a day. She worked in the office until midnight, or thereabouts.” Asked if she dated, she responded, “Oh no, I’m married to Theranos.”

Movies

Billy Evans, the hotel heir and father of Elizabeth Holmes’ two children, has become a central figure in Nathan Fielder’s documentary ‘You Can See Everything.’ Here’s what to know about his background, career and relationship with the disgraced Theranos founder.

The Theranos board of directors included luminaries such as former U.S. secretaries of State Henry Kissinger and George Shultz, and former U.S. Secretary of Defense James Mattis. Auletta said they seemed awed by Holmes: “They were talking about her like she was Beethoven, that she was this rare creature that maybe one in a century or maybe two in a century come along who really can change the world.”

Stanford University professor of medicine Phyllis Gardner said of Holmes, “She aligned herself with very powerful older men who seemed to succumb to a certain charm, and those powerful men could influence people in the government, the Department of Defense.”

In “You Can See Everything,” Evans appears to have a controlling dynamic with Holmes, whether it’s in the way she stirs her eggs or the posts published on her social media account while she’s in prison.

But the romantic and professional relationship between Holmes and former company president Sunny Balwani seemed to be the opposite. The two lived together in a Palo Alto condo. He was 49; she was 30.

“He talked about her in a very differential way,” Auletta said. Fortune Magazine writer Roger Perloff said Balwani called Holmes “the most important inventor of our times.” Theranos biochemist Doug Matje said, “Sunny saw her as this iconic figure that he could never be, and so I think he found this vehicle to advance himself in her, and she was on board for it, too.”

Movies

A former Theranos research engineer who worked closely with Elizabeth Holmes says that ‘You Can See Everything’ is misleading and definitely not a documentary.

A key sequence in “You Can See Everything” revolves around Holmes telling Fielder she has never told a lie, and his incredulous response.

But several Theranos staffers and journalists say Holmes was frequently deceptive and would lie repeatedly, especially when confronted with facts.

Perloff was incensed by one letter where Holmes said she did not realize he was writing a story about her.

“This was real lunacy,” he said. “I realized there was something wrong with her mind. I don’t know if she’s lying or has an unconscious self-protective reconstruction of reality that’s going on. But what’s coming out of her mouth is not mapping onto reality as you or I know it.”

Actual Article Body:
(Photo by DON EMMERT/AFP via Getty Images)

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), joined by a bipartisan group of twelve state attorneys general, sued to block a merger in a market that directly affects American families.

PlayPower, owned by private equity firm Platinum Equity, sought to acquire its closest competitor, BCI Burke. The companies compete head to head, particularly on smaller and mid-sized projects that are common for elementary schools, neighborhood parks, and community organizations. That competition has produced lower prices, better equipment options, and stronger service for buyers who often have limited leverage, the FTC argues.
